transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you for fitting me in. I... well, it’s a bit embarrassing to admit at my age, but I came because I just spend far, far too much of my day checking things. Not the stove or the front door locks—I know people always think of that when you talk about checking—but... well, it's my papers. My important papers and keepsakes. 

I have these labeled boxes, you see. Beautiful, sturdy archival ones I bought years ago when my late husband passed, just to keep everything properly organized. The birth certificates, the deed to the house, Arthur's old military records, photographs from when the children were little... and I just, I find myself opening the exact same folders, the same heavy oak drawers in the study, and those labeled boxes again and again and again. Just to make absolutely sure they are exactly where I left them. 

And the truly ridiculous thing is, I know they are there. I mean, I *just* checked them. I will look at the folder, run my hand over it, put it back, close the drawer, walk into the kitchen to put the kettle on for some tea, and before the water even begins to boil... I’m right back in the study, pulling open that very same drawer. It's like this nagging itch in my mind that they might have vanished or been misplaced in those three minutes. I just can't seem to stop myself, and it's taking up my whole day. It's terribly exhausting, really, because I have to look at every single item to feel settled, and then that settled feeling just disappears almost the moment I leave the room.
Do you find yourself having recurring, unwanted thoughts or images in your mind that you can't seem to get rid of, even when you're not checking your papers?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. It’s... it's quite bothersome, actually. Even when I’m nowhere near the study—say I’m just sitting in my armchair by the window, trying to enjoy the afternoon sun, or perhaps trying to read a chapter of a book, though my eyes aren't quite what they used to be—this thought will just pop into my head. It’s like a little gnat buzzing around that you simply can't swat away. 

I’ll be sitting there, perfectly comfortable, and suddenly I’ll think, "Oh, heavens, what if I accidentally threw away Arthur’s old tax papers from 1982 when I was sorting the mail last week?" Which is absurd, of course, because the mail goes on the kitchen counter and Arthur’s papers are in the blue box on the second shelf in the study. Or I’ll think, "Did I put my grandmother’s lemon cake recipe in the box with the utility bills instead of the family history box?" 

And the thing is, Doctor, I *know* I didn't. I am a very careful person. I always have been. When Arthur was alive, he used to say I was the only reason we never lost a single receipt. But even knowing that—even knowing better—the thought just keeps needling at me. It pokes and prods, and this dreadful feeling washes over me that I’ve done something terribly, terribly careless. That I’ve ruined our family history or lost something irreplaceable through sheer negligence. And I just can't seem to let the thought pass. It sits there, heavy in my chest, making me feel so guilty and anxious until I finally give in and go look. And then, well, then the whole checking business starts all over again, just like I was telling you. It really is a vicious cycle, isn't it? I just wish I could turn my brain off sometimes, just for a little while, so I wouldn't have to worry about whether a piece of paper from forty years ago is in the correct folder.

When you feel that anxiety or guilt about possibly misplacing something, does going to check the papers actually make you feel better, or does it just give you a little peace for a short time before the worry comes back?

Well, it is exactly as you described, Doctor. It’s just... a little sliver of peace. A very, very short-term peace. When I finally give in—and I do try to resist, I really try to just sit in my chair and read—but when I finally walk back into the study and pull open those heavy oak drawers... well, like I was telling you when I first came in, I spend just far, far too much of my day doing exactly this. I open the exact same folders, the same labeled boxes, again and again and again, just to make absolutely sure those important papers and keepsakes are exactly where I left them. 

And for a second, just one brief second when I see them sitting there, perfectly safe and neatly filed... I feel this tremendous wave of relief. My chest loosens up, and I think to myself, 'There, you see? Everything is perfectly fine. You were just being a silly old woman.' 

But then I put the lid back on the box—they have those very snug-fitting lids, you know, the archival ones, to keep the dust and moisture out, which is so terribly important for old photographs and documents—and I push the drawer shut. And I kid you not, Doctor, I haven't even made it out into the hallway before the doubt creeps right back in. I’ll stop in my tracks and think, 'Wait, did I actually see the deed just now, or did I only see the manila folder for the deed?' Or, 'Heavens, what if I accidentally pulled Arthur's discharge papers out and dropped them on the floor when I was checking the folder next to it?' 

And so, there I am, turning right back around to open the same folders and boxes all over again, even though I had quite literally just checked them a few minutes—sometimes a few seconds—before! It’s a dreadful cycle. The relief is so incredibly brief, and then I'm right back to spending my whole afternoon opening and closing things. I'm honestly surprised the hinges on those drawers haven't completely worn out by now. It just never seems to be enough to make the worry stay away for good.
Have you ever felt the need to check or redo things other than your papers or keepsakes, like appliances, locks, or other items around the house?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I know that's what people usually think of, isn't it? When you hear about someone checking things, it's always the stove, or the iron, or making sure the front door is locked three times before bed. My sister Margaret, bless her heart, she used to be terrible about the iron. She would call me from the grocery store in a panic, absolutely convinced she'd left it plugged in and the house was going to burn down. But no, I've never really struggled with that sort of thing. 

I suppose I do make sure the door is locked at night, but just the once, like any sensible person living alone would do. And the stove... well, I hardly cook these days anyway. Mostly just tea, or heating up a bit of soup. I don't have those terrible thoughts about the house burning down or someone breaking in. It's really just... just the papers. Just my boxes and my folders. 

It's strange, isn't it? That my mind gets so terribly stuck on Arthur's old tax returns from the eighties, but I don't give a second thought to whether the back door is bolted. But no, it's just the study. That's the only place I get that dreadful, itching feeling that I have to go back and look. Everything else in the house is quite peaceful, really. It's just those papers that give me such grief.

Do you ever find yourself doing anything else over and over again, not just checking the papers, but maybe counting, repeating certain words in your head, or performing specific actions in a certain way to make yourself feel better or prevent something bad from happening?

Well, no, not really. I mean, counting? Repeating words? Oh, goodness, no. It’s funny you should mention counting, though, because Arthur—my late husband, you know—he was an accountant, so counting was practically his life’s work. He used to sit at the dining room table with his adding machine, the kind with the paper roll that would just go *click-clack-click-clack* for hours on end, especially around tax season. But me? No, I’ve never been much for numbers. 

And as for repeating words in my head... well, I do sometimes get a song stuck in my head, like that old Perry Como tune, "Catch a Falling Star," but that’s just normal, isn't it? Everyone gets a little tune stuck now and then. But I don't do it on purpose, and certainly not to stop something terrible from happening. 

I don't have any little rituals like that. I don't tap the doorframe three times, or have to put my left shoe on before my right shoe, or anything of that sort. I know some people do that—I read an article once in *Reader's Digest* about a woman who had to turn the light switch on and off exactly seven times before she could leave a room, which sounds absolutely exhausting, quite frankly. But no, I don't do anything like that at all. 

It really is just the papers, Doctor. Just the awful, nagging feeling that I’ve misplaced a deed, or a birth certificate, or one of the children's old report cards from 1964. If it weren't for those boxes in the study, I’d be perfectly fine. I just sit and read, or watch the birds at the feeder—I have a lovely little family of cardinals that visits the suet feeder I put out on the patio—and I don't feel the need to count them or do anything special. I just watch them. So, no, none of those other things you mentioned. Just the endless checking of those files.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms are highly specific to checking behaviors related to important documents without other compulsions or obsessions, which is consistent with F42.2 (Obsessive-compulsive disorder, with predominance of compulsive acts [rituals]). Other subtypes under F42 have been ruled out based on absence of generalized obsessions, mixed obsessions and rituals, or unspecified features.
